1057.name: Drew Allar
1057.headline: Steelers Bet A Third-Rounder On The Arm Aaron Rodgers Never Had To Wait For
1057.subhead: Drew Allar arrived in Latrobe billed as a raw project, then spent August outplaying the expectation and forcing Pittsburgh to think about 2027 sooner than it planned.

measurables.combineNote: Allar threw at the 2026 Combine in Indianapolis but did not run the 40, jump, or do agility drills, so there is no athletic testing profile on him at all. The evaluation was always the throwing session and the medical: he was seven months removed from the broken ankle that ended his final Penn State season, and teams came away satisfied he was a physically gifted thrower with a big, easy arm.

collegeCareer: Allar was the No. 1 quarterback and a top-three overall prospect in the 2022 class, a five-star out of Medina, Ohio who arrived at Penn State as the most significant quarterback recruit in program history. He redshirted behind Sean Clifford in name only, appearing in 10 games as a freshman and opening his career with an FBS-record 311 pass attempts without an interception, breaking Robert Griffin III's mark. That set the template for the whole run: extraordinary care with the football, a heavy arm, and a maddening reluctance to let it rip into tight windows.

The 2023 season made him a starter and a punchline in equal measure — 2,631 yards, 25 touchdowns and just two interceptions, but 59.9 percent completions and a bottom-tier deep-ball hit rate that had Penn State fans calling for the offense to be blown up. It was, and 2024 was the payoff: 3,327 yards at 8.4 per attempt, 24 touchdowns, a 66.5 percent completion rate and a run to the College Football Playoff semifinals. He also ran for meaningful yardage across his career (732 yards, 12 touchdowns), a bigger part of his game than the pocket-statue label suggested.

The 2025 season was supposed to be the coronation for a preseason top-two team and instead became the collapse that reshaped the program. Allar's numbers slipped (1,100 yards, eight touchdowns, three interceptions in six games) before a broken ankle against Northwestern in October ended his college career on a stretcher-and-cart note. He finished first all-time at Penn State in completion percentage (63.2) and interception rate (1.3), third in touchdown passes (61) and fourth in passing yards (7,402), and is the only FBS quarterback since 1956 with 900-plus attempts, 50-plus touchdowns and 12 or fewer picks.

The scouting file is consistent: prototype size, elite arm strength that Penn State's offense rarely asked him to use, excellent decision-making by volume, but late trigger, inconsistent accuracy on layered throws, and a habit of taking the checkdown when the shot was there. He never had a signature comeback win, and the injury robbed him of the chance to change that.

draftDayStory: Pittsburgh took Allar at No. 76 overall on the second night — Round 3, the twelfth pick of the round, exactly where the KTC draft-capital line has it. It was the Steelers' third pick of a four-selection Friday that also produced Alabama receiver Germie Bernard, Georgia cornerback Daylen Everette and Iowa guard Gennings Dunker, and it continued a pattern: Kenny Pickett out of Pitt in 2022, Will Howard out of Ohio State in 2025, now Allar out of Penn State. Local arms, mid-round money, no franchise commitment.

The context matters more than the slot. Pittsburgh drafted Allar while still waiting on Aaron Rodgers to decide whether he wanted a 22nd season, which meant the pick was made as a 2027 bet rather than a 2026 solution. A player who was a projected first-rounder entering 2025 was available at 76 because of the ankle, the six-game sample and four years of tape that never quite matched the arm. Mike McCarthy, in his first year running his hometown team and with a long history of developing quarterbacks, got a project with a prototype body at a discount.
whyTheyDraftedHim: Prototype frame and arm talent: 6-5 with the kind of velocity McCarthy's staff believes can be unlocked once the footwork is rebuilt, and a four-year Big Ten starter's résumé of pre-snap command.

McCarthy's development track record was the entire premise of the pick — the Steelers put Allar through a 'profile tape' evaluation at rookie minicamp and immediately began adjusting his fundamentals.
Elite ball security: 61 touchdowns to 13 interceptions and the lowest interception rate in Penn State history is exactly the risk profile a McCarthy offense wants from a young quarterback.
Cost and timing: with Rodgers on a one-year runway and Mason Rudolph a known bridge, a third-round arm is the cheapest possible way to have a 2027 candidate already in the building.
Underrated mobility — 732 career rushing yards and 12 touchdowns — plus a willingness to run in the red zone, which showed up on his first NFL possession.

campNotes.note: Allar was the last Steeler off the field on the first day of camp at Saint Vincent College, staying to sign autographs; the framing all week was that he was a 'quick study' being asked to absorb a completely new system after four years in one college offense.

On the first padded practice in Latrobe, Allar made the splash throw of the day — a 55-yard touchdown to Cole Burgess in seven-on-sevens — and hit Max Hurleman over the middle on fourth down in team period. BTSC's verdict: he had played 'better than anticipated' through the first week, with the expectation having been that he would look raw.

Pittsburgh's first unofficial depth chart listed Allar as QB4 behind Aaron Rodgers, Mason Rudolph and Will Howard — exactly the pecking order McCarthy described early in camp, and a reminder that practice buzz had not yet moved the official ladder.

At the annual night practice at Latrobe Memorial Stadium in front of roughly 8,500 fans, Allar delivered his best passing display of the summer after an inconsistent stretch that included a widely circulated clip of him missing the practice net: a 25-yard seam throw to Robert Tonyan, a 30-yard sideline strike to Brandon Smith into tight coverage, then a 20-yard crosser to Smith. He credited picking Rodgers' brain on the deep ball a week earlier.

Preseason debut against Green Bay: 10-of-13 for 154 yards with touchdown passes to Kaden Wetjen and Riley Nowakowski plus a 3-yard touchdown run in a 28-9 win, entering to 'Drewwww' chants. He finished the game and was the story of the night.

campNotes.source: Steelers.com / New York Jets box score
campNotes.note: With Rodgers and Rudolph resting, Allar played the second half of a 17-0 shutout loss to the Jets and went 11-of-23 for 110 yards with no touchdowns and no turnovers, his best moment a 39-yard throw to Lake McCree. Progress, in his own words, was not linear.

Team sources told Dulac that the decision to keep both Allar and Howard on the 53-man roster was made even before the Jets game, meaning the Allar-Howard competition is about 2027 positioning rather than roster survival.

beatQuotes.quote: He's a physically gifted thrower of the football, but he's no different than any other young quarterback that I've had the opportunity to work with. We're able to just adjust some fundamentals that we think will help him. He made a very good first impression.
beatQuotes.attribution: Mike McCarthy, Steelers head coach, Steelers.com, May 9

beatQuotes.quote: It's a lot of room for me to grow. A lot of football to learn. A lot of basics and nuances of the game. I've learned a lot from a QB fundamental standpoint already and X's and O's standpoint.

There will be one more preseason game to determine how many quarterbacks Steelers coach Mike McCarthy will keep on his 53-man roster. But he doesn't need another game to know this: Will Howard and Drew Allar will be on the team.
I just need to do a better job, especially early in drives, taking what's given.

1057.depthChart: QB4 on the official preseason depth chart: Aaron Rodgers is the starter, Mason Rudolph is the veteran QB2, and Will Howard is listed third despite being outplayed by Allar for most of camp. Per the Post-Gazette, all three young quarterbacks make the 53, so Allar spends 2026 as an inactive-to-third-string developmental arm with the real competition — for the job Rodgers vacates after this season — starting in 2027.
whyHeCouldSucceed: Rodgers has told the organization this is his last season, so the Steelers' 2027 starting job is genuinely open, and Allar has already outperformed the only internal competitor for it (Will Howard) through a full camp and two preseason games.

Mike McCarthy is one of the league's most accomplished quarterback developers and rebuilt Allar's fundamentals from the first day of rookie minicamp; the arm talent that made him a five-star was never the question, the mechanics and processing were.
He has a year to learn behind Aaron Rodgers as a de facto redshirt, with no pressure to play badly early — the exact developmental runway mid-round quarterbacks almost never get.
The preseason opener showed the traits that translate: quick command of a pro system, two touchdown throws, a red-zone scramble score, and the pocket poise of a 45-game Big Ten starter.
Draft capital is cheap in dynasty terms but organizational investment is not — Pittsburgh has now spent back-to-back drafts acquiring young arms and has publicly committed roster spots to both.
whyHeCouldFail: He is the fourth quarterback on the roster right now and could easily throw zero regular-season passes in 2026, which is a full year of dead dynasty roster space.
The 2027 job may never be his: Pittsburgh is widely expected to add a quarterback in the 2027 draft, and Allar and Howard could both be reduced to camp bodies for whoever that is.

The college tape has real flaws — late trigger, inconsistent accuracy on layered throws, a deep-ball hit rate that never matched the arm — and one good preseason night does not fix four years of that.
His final college season ended with a broken ankle after a six-game statistical regression, so the last extended live football he played was bad, and there is no athletic testing to lean on.
The Jets game was the counterweight to the Packers game: 11-of-23 for 110 yards and no points in a shutout, exactly the uneven ceiling that dropped him to Round 3.
fantasyOutlook: For 2026, project nothing. Rodgers is the starter, Rudolph is the emergency plan, and Allar's realistic path to snaps is a two-injury scenario in a run-heavy offense that would not be built around him anyway. Zero-point seasons are the base case. Everything about his value is 2027: a Rodgers-less roster, a coach who drafted him and rebuilt his throwing motion, and an offense with Germie Bernard, DK Metcalf and a competent line already in place. In superflex leagues, that is precisely the profile you stash — cheap capital, no immediate cost to your lineup, and a plausible path to a starting NFL job within 12 months.

Price him as a late-second to early-third-round rookie pick in superflex .5 PPR, which lines up with a board rank near 26 and a consensus rank in the 40s. The gap between those two numbers is the whole argument: superflex managers pay for the possibility of a starting quarterback, redraft-flavored rankers pay for 2026 production, and Allar has none of the latter. Buy him if your quarterback room is set and you can wait; do not spend a pick you need to fill a starting lineup this year. If Pittsburgh drafts a quarterback high in 2027, his dynasty value goes to near zero overnight.
1057.comp: A taller Mason Rudolph if it goes badly, Brock Purdy-lite in terms of situation-dependence if it goes well — a caretaker with a much better arm than either, whose value hinges entirely on whether the staff that rebuilt him also gets to hand him the job.
1057.bottomLine: A pure 2027 lottery ticket with real arm talent and the league's best-positioned developmental runway; take him in the late second or third round of a superflex rookie draft and forget about him for a year.

1022.name: Ted Hurst
1022.headline: Tampa Bay Went Shopping For Mike Evans' Size And Came Back With A Sun Belt Secret
1022.subhead: A Division II transfer who ran 4.42 at 6-4, Ted Hurst spent August high-pointing footballs in Baker Mayfield's practices and then learned how unforgiving the preseason can be.
1022.draftPick: Round 3, Pick 20 (No. 84 overall), Tampa Bay Buccaneers

measurables.combineNote: Hurst tested like the athlete his tape suggested: 4.42 in the 40 at 6-foot-4 and 206 pounds, a 36.5-inch vertical, and a broad jump of 11-3 that led all wide receivers in Indianapolis. He skipped the bench, three-cone and shuttle. Georgia State listed him at 6-3, 195; the Combine numbers are the real ones, and he has since been listed around 210 in Tampa.

collegeCareer: Hurst grew up in Savannah, played cornerback as a high school senior and got no Division I offers, landing at Valdosta State as a non-scholarship receiver. Two years of Division II football produced 60 catches for 1,027 yards and 10 touchdowns at 17.1 per grab — enough big-play tape to earn a Sun Belt transfer, not enough to make him a known prospect.

Georgia State turned him into one. In 2024 he caught 56 passes for 961 yards and nine touchdowns at a preposterous 17.2 per catch on 97 targets, and in 2025 he added 71 catches for 1,004 yards and six scores on 126 targets for a team that finished 1-11 and 0-8 in the conference. He is one of only four FBS receivers with 950-plus receiving yards in each of the last two seasons, and he did it as the entire offense on a bad team, with defenses knowing exactly where the ball was going.

The 'small-school' tag never survived contact. He went 7-128-2 against Vanderbilt in 2024 and 7-71 against the same SEC defense in 2025, hung a 10-172-2 line on Murray State and a 10-165-1 on Coastal Carolina, and then answered the level-of-competition question directly with a strong week of Senior Bowl practices in January. Bruce Feldman had already put him on The Athletic's college football Freaks List for the size-speed-explosion combination.

The knocks are technical, not physical: he is a raw route runner who wins with stride length and speed rather than deception, and he can be soft at the catch point when he has to come back to the football or dig a ball out below the waist. Twenty-five career touchdowns across four seasons and two levels say the ball skills at the top of his catch radius are real.

draftDayStory: Hurst was Tampa Bay's first offensive pick of the 2026 draft, taken 84th overall in the third round after the Buccaneers traded down slightly and picked up an extra fifth-rounder. Jason Licht had spent the first two picks on defense (Rueben Bain Jr. in Round 1, Josiah Trotter in Round 2) and the third night on a receiver room that was already deep — Emeka Egbuka, Chris Godwin Jr., Jalen McMillan, Tez Johnson — but conspicuously short one thing: the big-bodied X receiver Mike Evans played for a decade before signing with San Francisco in March. The slot matches the KTC draft-capital line exactly (Round 3, twelfth-to-twentieth range of the round, No. 84 overall).

Tampa Bay was explicit that this was about replacing an archetype rather than a person. Vice president of player personnel Mike Biehl called Hurst a 'raw player' with a lot to improve in his route running while making clear the appeal was a 6-4, 210-pound receiver who runs in the 4.4s with contested-catch ball skills. Nobody in the building projected an immediate featured role — Biehl's framing was that Hurst would earn whatever he was ready for.
whyTheyDraftedHim: Direct answer to the Mike Evans vacancy at the X spot: Tampa Bay wanted the size-speed archetype back in the room even while insisting they were not replacing the man himself.
Rare testing profile — 4.42 at 6-4 with a class-best 11-3 broad jump — which put him on The Athletic's Freaks List and made him a Day 2 athlete regardless of conference.
'He's just kind of checked the boxes every step of the way' (Biehl): a no-offer high schooler to Division II walk-on to back-to-back 950-yard FBS seasons to a strong Senior Bowl week.
Contested-catch and vertical ball skills that fit a Zac Robinson offense looking for a true field-stretcher opposite Egbuka and Godwin.
Room to develop without being needed immediately, which is exactly how Tampa Bay has historically handled receiver draft picks.

campNotes.note: With Jalen McMillan, Emeka Egbuka and Chris Godwin Jr. all held out of Tuesday's practice, Hurst became Baker Mayfield's go-to target and made what Todd Bowles called 'a heck of a play,' with Bowles emphasizing that Mayfield already trusts him to be where he's supposed to be.

In the closing two-minute period of the second joint practice against the Jets, Hurst was one of three players (with Cade Otton and Ayden Garnes) singled out for standout plays, contributing a big gain on the drive that ended in Mayfield's touchdown to Otton.

After Egbuka's toe injury, Hurst was described as 'one of the biggest standouts of training camp,' consistently making difficult catches and winning downfield, and was effectively penciled into the top four of the receiver room alongside Egbuka, Godwin and McMillan.

Preseason debut at the Jets with Egbuka, Godwin and McMillan all out: Hurst worked as the de facto No. 1 receiver and caught two of six targets for 19 yards from Connor Bazelak, dropping a goal-line slant thrown behind him and losing another catch to a replay review. Reviewers liked the route running, flagged his lack of physicality at the catch point.

Mayfield said Hurst is 'growing quickly,' is playing fast rather than thinking, and is high-pointing the ball and winning one-on-one matchups — and that he is confident in where the rookie is at heading into the Chiefs game.

With Mayfield and Jake Browning playing and Egbuka and Godwin out, Hurst's second preseason game was a dud: zero catches and a 15-yard unsportsmanlike-conduct penalty that helped kill Tampa Bay's opening drive in a 16-15 win over Kansas City. Pewter Report listed him first among the most disappointing Buccaneers that night.

beatQuotes.quote: Baker trusts him. He knows he goes where he needs to go with the football. Ted was open at the right time, so we know he's got a good vertical and he's got very good hands. He made a heck of a play.
beatQuotes.attribution: Todd Bowles, Buccaneers head coach, Buccaneers.com, Aug 5

beatQuotes.quote: Ted is growing quickly. He is picking things up and is really fast... he is high-pointing the ball and is really taking advantage of his one-on-one matchups and just contested catches and things like that that when you are a bigger receiver at 6'4, you want to be a safety blanket for those 50/50 balls, and so I am really confident in where Ted is at.
beatQuotes.attribution: Baker Mayfield, Buccaneers quarterback, Buccaneers.com, Aug 18

beatQuotes.quote: We're never ever going to try and replace Mike, but you do try to replace size and speed, which Mike had, and we think that Ted has that too. He's just kind of a raw player, but he's a big, fast, athletic guy that's willing to learn.
beatQuotes.attribution: Mike Biehl, Buccaneers VP of player personnel, Buccaneers.com, Apr 25

1022.depthChart: Fourth in a crowded room and climbing: Emeka Egbuka, Chris Godwin Jr. and Jalen McMillan opened as the starting trio on Tampa Bay's first unofficial depth chart, with Hurst the clear No. 4 and the primary X-receiver body behind them. Egbuka (toe), Godwin and McMillan (knee) all missed preseason time, which handed Hurst first-team reps all August — and both Godwin's and McMillan's injury histories mean that door is likely to keep opening in-season.
whyHeCouldSucceed: He is the only receiver on the roster built like the departed Mike Evans, and Tampa Bay drafted him specifically to play the X spot in Zac Robinson's offense, so his snaps do not depend on beating out a similar player.
The quarterback is already vouching for him publicly in August; Mayfield's trust plus a 6-4 frame in the red zone is the fastest route to cheap touchdowns for a rookie.
Chris Godwin (age, coming off major injuries) and Jalen McMillan (knee) both have real availability risk, and Hurst has already taken de facto No. 1 receiver reps every time they sat this month.
The athletic profile is genuinely rare — 4.42 at 6-4 with a class-leading broad jump — and back-to-back 950-yard FBS seasons on a 1-11 team means the production was not scheme-inflated.
Third-round capital plus an unusually loud camp buzz cycle (including Evans comparisons from beat writers) means the staff will keep feeding him opportunities to earn a role.
whyHeCouldFail: The room is stacked with Egbuka ascending, Godwin still a target hog when healthy, McMillan and Tez Johnson ahead of him in the pecking order; a fourth receiver in Tampa Bay may see 40 targets.
His two preseason games were a warning: two catches on six targets with a goal-line drop, then zero catches and a 15-yard unsportsmanlike penalty against Kansas City.
Scouts and coaches agree he is a raw route runner who wins on stride length; if the release package and break precision do not develop, he becomes a pure deep-ball specialist.
Physicality at the catch point on anything below his chest is a real flaw — coming back to the football and digging out low throws is exactly what an NFL X receiver has to do.
Level-of-competition risk is not fully retired: a Division II transfer who dominated the Sun Belt has a longer adjustment curve than a Power Four alpha, and Tampa Bay has said as much.
fantasyOutlook: The 2026 baseline is a No. 4 receiver in a good offense: think 30-45 targets, 20-30 catches, 300-400 yards and a couple of touchdowns if everyone stays healthy. But nothing about this receiver room stays healthy. Godwin has missed significant time in each of the last two seasons and McMillan is already working back from a knee issue; a single absence pushes Hurst into a two-receiver rotation with Mayfield throwing him fades. He is a weekly stash rather than a weekly start, with the kind of week-winning spike upside a 6-4 field-stretcher gets in the red zone.

In a superflex .5 PPR dynasty league, Hurst is a fair second-round rookie pick — the market has him around rookie 20 on consensus boards and 27 on KTC, and both are reasonable. He is the highest-capital receiver in this tier with a defined role waiting for him and a quarterback already publicly bought in. Pay for the archetype, not the 2026 box score: the bet is that by 2027 Godwin is gone, McMillan is a slot, and Hurst is the outside-the-numbers starter on an offense that has produced top-24 fantasy receivers every year Mayfield has been there.
1022.comp: Nico Collins is the flattering version and Christian Watson the honest one — same size-speed outlier profile and vertical dominance, same questions about route nuance and week-to-week reliability.
1022.bottomLine: Buy him in the second round of your rookie draft as the X receiver Tampa Bay drafted him to be; he is one Godwin or McMillan injury away from 70 targets, and one bad August game should not change that.

1040.name: Emmett Johnson
1040.headline: Nebraska’s Workhorse Finds A Crowded Kansas City Backfield To Conquer
1040.subhead: A record-setting Nebraska season earned Emmett Johnson a Day 3 runway, but Kansas City’s crowded backfield makes immediate touches precious.
1040.draftPick: Round 5, Pick 21 (No. 161 overall), Kansas City Chiefs

measurables.combineNote: Johnson tested at the 2026 NFL Combine, with published results listing a 4.56-second forty, 1.59-second split, 35.5-inch vertical, 10-foot broad jump and 16 bench-press reps. A March Pro Day listing also credits him with a 4.50-second forty and 1.60-second split.

collegeCareer: Johnson arrived at Nebraska as Minnesota’s 2021 Mr. Football and spent his redshirt freshman season learning how to turn limited opportunity into reliable production. He played 12 games in 2023, starting six of the final seven, and ran for 411 yards on 90 carries while adding seven catches. His 2024 season expanded the toolbox: 598 rushing yards, 39 receptions and 908 all-purpose yards, with the receiving work signaling that he was more than a committee runner.

In 2025, Johnson became Nebraska’s offensive engine. He led the Big Ten with 1,451 rushing yards and paced all FBS running backs with 46 catches, finishing with 1,821 scrimmage yards and 15 total touchdowns in 12 regular-season games. The workload was enormous, but so was the versatility: Johnson ran inside, created on cuts, caught checkdowns and screens, and accounted for 40.7 percent of Nebraska’s regular-season yardage. He opted out of the bowl after declaring for the draft.

draftDayStory: Kansas City traded up with Pittsburgh to take Johnson at No. 161, the 21st pick of Round 5. The official Chiefs draft tracker and post-draft personnel recap confirm the slot, which matches KTC’s Round 5, Pick 21 designation; there is no draft-capital discrepancy.

The landing spot was a bet on production surviving translation. Kansas City personnel officials said they were shocked Johnson remained available, while his post-draft message was characteristically direct: he had been overlooked before and only needed an opportunity. He now enters an Andy Reid offense that values backs who can run, catch and stay useful without the ball.
whyTheyDraftedHim: He produced like a featured back and a slot receiver in 2025, pairing 1,451 rushing yards with 46 catches and 1,821 scrimmage yards.
His vision, patience and sharp lateral cuts give Kansas City a runner who can create when blocking is imperfect rather than simply waiting for clean daylight.
He already demonstrated enough receiving polish to threaten for third-down work, a valuable trait behind a starting back whose workload will need managing.
Johnson’s competitive temperament and willingness to contribute on special teams fit a roster-building plan that demands Day 3 picks earn multiple jobs.

campNotes.note: At the Chiefs’ second rookie-and-quarterback camp practice, Johnson was the first player on the field. He emphasized conditioning, detail work and an intention to be the toughest player on the field.

Johnson consistently arrived before practice and used the JUGS machine to sharpen his hands. The early routine reinforced Kansas City’s view that his path to playing time runs through receiving and pass-protection growth.

In the preseason opener against the Rams, Johnson handled 12 carries for 59 yards and caught all three targets for 10 yards. He led Chiefs backs with 35 snaps, and a holding penalty erased a touchdown.

Running backs coach DeMarco Murray praised Johnson’s physical running after the Rams game but identified footwork and route depth as cleanup items. The assessment captured both his immediate utility and his rookie limitations.

Johnson ran seven times for 25 yards and a touchdown against Tampa Bay, caught one of two targets for 10 yards and returned two kickoffs for 51 yards. He was the third Chiefs back to receive a touch behind Kenneth Walker and Emari Demercado.

beatQuotes.quote: He ran the ball extremely hard, physical behind his pads.
We have to clean up some foot work details, some route depth.
He did a nice job with it and ran hard and aggressive.
beatQuotes.attribution: Andy Reid, Kansas City Star, Aug 15

1040.depthChart: Kenneth Walker is the clear starter. The unofficial chart initially placed Emari Demercado second and Johnson third, with Brashard Smith also competing, but Johnson’s 35-snap preseason opener and strong rushing work have pushed him into the serious RB2 conversation. He appears more likely to make the roster than not, yet pass protection remains the swing skill separating a backup role from a weekly active spot.
whyHeCouldSucceed: Johnson’s 2025 workload showed he can carry an offense without becoming one-dimensional. He creates with patience, presses the line before cutting, and has enough receiving experience to stay on the field in spread formations.

Kansas City’s offense rewards backs who see creases quickly and finish runs with force. Johnson’s vision and contact balance were evident immediately in preseason, where he repeatedly turned modest blocking into efficient gains.
His receiving profile is more than a draft-day talking point. Forty-six catches in 2025 and a daily JUGS routine give him a credible route to third-down snaps while he learns the protection system.
If Walker misses time, Johnson has the college volume and all-purpose résumé to handle a meaningful share rather than functioning as a purely situational replacement.
whyHeCouldFail: A crowded room can bury a rookie even after a productive preseason. Walker owns the lead role, Demercado brings veteran pass-protection trust, and Smith offers return-game value that can influence active-day decisions.

Murray’s criticism of Johnson’s footwork and route depth points to the central risk: explosive college production does not matter if the staff cannot trust him to execute assignments in the passing game.
His 200-pound frame and Nebraska workload invite questions about whether his college contact balance will hold against NFL tacklers without a meaningful efficiency drop.
Kansas City may prefer a veteran committee while Johnson learns, leaving his rookie touches dependent on injuries, game script and special-teams readiness rather than talent alone.
fantasyOutlook: Johnson is a handcuff with real contingency value, not a player to treat as an immediate weekly starter. A reasonable 2026 expectation is roughly 70-110 touches if Walker stays healthy, with a path to more if Johnson wins the passing-down trust that Demercado currently owns. The rookie-draft price is fair around pick 28 in superflex formats, especially in .5 PPR where his receiving ability gives him a floor beyond pure early-down work. KTC’s 2,537 superflex value and Tier 8 label reflect the uncertainty, while FantasyPros’ consensus rookie rank of 17 is a useful reminder that the talent profile outruns the depth-chart rank.

Dynasty managers should buy the player only at the right discount. Walker’s contract and Kansas City’s committee options suppress 2026 volume, but Johnson’s age, four-year production and receiving résumé create a credible 2027 breakout window. He is a strong late-first/early-second rookie selection in superflex leagues, with more appeal to contenders who can wait than to teams needing immediate lineup points.
1040.comp: A more compact, less explosive version of James White, with Nebraska’s volume showing he can handle far more early-down work.
1040.bottomLine: Draft Johnson as a premium handcuff and patient dynasty stash, not as Kansas City’s Week 1 starter. His route to value is clear: pass protection, receiving detail and one Walker injury could turn a Day 3 pick into a league-winning contingency back.

1031.name: Kaytron Allen
1031.headline: Kaytron Allen’s Bowling-Ball Style Earns A Washington Roster Opening
1031.subhead: Penn State’s all-time rushing leader brings short-yardage power to a crowded Commanders backfield and has forced his way into the roster math.

measurables.combineNote: Allen did not record athletic testing at either the 2026 NFL Combine or Penn State Pro Day. Reports say he opted out of physical testing, leaving his timed speed and jumping numbers unknown.

collegeCareer: Allen entered Penn State alongside Nicholas Singleton and immediately became half of one of the nation’s most productive backfield duos. He ran for 867 yards and 10 touchdowns as a true freshman, followed that with 902 yards in 2023, and crossed 1,000 yards for the first time in 2024. His value was rooted in patience, square shoulders and contact balance: Allen found creases in heavy boxes and routinely turned first contact into a few more necessary yards.

The senior season delivered his best efficiency and his clearest professional case. Allen ran for 1,303 yards at 6.2 yards per carry and scored 15 times in 12 games, finishing as Penn State’s all-time leader in carries and rushing yards with 4,180 yards on 769 attempts. He was not a high-volume receiver, but he caught 70 career passes and showed enough ball skill to keep defenses honest. Washington drafted the identity as much as the numbers: a compact, physical back who can make short yardage an offensive advantage.

draftDayStory: Washington selected Allen with No. 187 overall, the sixth pick of Round 6. The Commanders’ official draft tracker and Penn State coverage confirm the slot, exactly matching KTC’s Round 6, Pick 6 designation; there is no draft-capital discrepancy.

The pick gave Washington a distinctly different back from its quicker, more versatile options. Allen’s 4,180 career rushing yards made him Penn State’s all-time leader, but his appeal was more specific than the record: he can lower his pads, survive congested lanes and make short-yardage football feel repeatable.
whyTheyDraftedHim: He owns the Penn State career records for rushing yards and attempts, giving Washington a proven workload profile against Big Ten competition.
His patience and vision work in heavy boxes; the Commanders cited his ability to find dirty yards and keep drives alive as a central reason for the selection.
Allen brings a short, dense frame and true pile-moving power that complements the burst and receiving ability elsewhere in Washington’s backfield.
His willingness to play through contact and contribute on teams gives a sixth-round pick a practical route to active-day value.

campNotes.note: Allen took the field for his first Commanders training camp and said the NFL game moved faster than college. He described using rookie minicamp, OTAs and mandatory minicamp to adjust before the full camp workload.

During a blocking drill, Allen rattled the goalposts and said his strength rating could be higher. The moment fit the early camp evaluation: a physically confident rookie still trying to prove that his power translates against NFL bodies.

With the pads on, observers described Allen as a punishing runner who was difficult to bring down and a more credible receiving threat than expected. The report said his roster position looked increasingly secure, though the competition was still early.
Allen led Washington in its preseason win over Miami with 23 carries for 85 yards and a one-yard touchdown. He acknowledged a slow start but said he adjusted as the game progressed.

With Rachaad White absent, Allen received extra work behind Jacory Croskey-Merritt and produced several solid runs, including one that reached the second level. He also lost a rep for a tackle behind the line from Javon Kinlaw.

Allen led Washington’s rushing attempts again against Detroit, carrying 10 times for 30 yards and catching his lone target for no gain. The workload reinforced his standing even as the offense managed only 35 rushing yards.

beatQuotes.quote: Kaytron finishing the game with a first down and a touchdown towards the end, those are the physical style runs we'd expect from him.
He has true move-the-line-of-scrimmage pile push.
I'm telling you, man, I have not seen somebody here break tackles as cleanly as he does.

1031.depthChart: Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White are ahead of Allen, with White the preferred passing-game option and Croskey-Merritt the more explosive lead-back candidate. Jerome Ford moved to injured reserve after his hamstring injury, while Jeremy McNichols’ quad injury and Robert Henry Jr.’s uneven second preseason game improved Allen’s roster odds. By Aug. 24 projections, Allen was a likely 53-man selection, but his early role is most naturally short-yardage, red-zone and committee work.
whyHeCouldSucceed: Allen’s defining skill is unusually dependable in the situations that decide drives. He stays square, sees the crease, lowers his pads and keeps moving after contact, giving Washington a reliable answer for third-and-short and goal-line snaps.

The Commanders have openly wanted more physicality in the running game. Allen’s style matches that mandate, and his preseason workload shows the staff is willing to let him establish rhythm rather than limiting him to token carries.
His vision prevents a slow offensive line from completely dictating the result. Against Detroit, he turned a four-yard loss into a one-yard gain on one play and repeatedly salvaged blocked-up runs.

Injury-created opportunity has moved him from sixth-round afterthought to likely roster player. Once active, his short-yardage specialization can earn touches even when Croskey-Merritt and White remain healthy.
whyHeCouldFail: Allen lacks verified athletic testing after opting out of the Combine and Pro Day, leaving teams and fantasy managers without a clean speed baseline and reinforcing concerns about NFL separation and breakaway ability.

Washington’s top two backs offer more obvious explosive-play or receiving value. If Croskey-Merritt and White stay healthy, Allen may be limited to matchup-specific carries instead of a stable weekly workload.
His 2025 receiving line was only 18 catches for 68 yards, and a sixth-round rookie cannot afford assignment errors if he wants to displace veterans on third down.
A crowded room remains dangerous despite injuries. McNichols has years of trust in the system, and Robert Henry’s special-teams contributions could still affect the final roster count.
fantasyOutlook: Allen is a late-round dynasty bet whose value rose sharply during August but still depends on role clarity. A reasonable 2026 projection is 50-90 touches with touchdown and short-yardage upside, plus a larger workload if Washington’s top backs miss time. In superflex .5 PPR rookie drafts, the fair price is around the 29th rookie slot: he is more attractive than his sixth-round capital suggests, but his limited receiving résumé and uncertain snap share keep him out of the premium tiers. KTC’s 2,517 superflex value and Tier 8 ranking fit that risk-reward profile, while FantasyPros’ consensus rookie rank of 24 reflects the preseason momentum.

The dynasty case is role-based rather than purely talent-based. Allen could become Washington’s preferred early-down and goal-line back if his physicality survives the regular season, but his long-term ceiling is capped unless the receiving work expands. He is a sensible late-second-round superflex pick for managers seeking cheap touchdown access and a strong bench handcuff, not a player to force into the lineup before the Commanders’ committee settles.
1031.comp: Stephen Davis with a smaller frame, built around square downhill runs, contact balance and short-yardage authority.
1031.bottomLine: Allen has played his way from roster bubble to likely 53-man back, but fantasy managers should price him as a committee power back. Draft him late in superflex rookie drafts for touchdown equity and contingency volume, not a guaranteed weekly role.

1015.name: Elijah Sarratt
1015.headline: Waffle House Comes Home: Baltimore's Fourth-Rounder Says He's Always Open
1015.subhead: A no-star recruit who won a national title and led the FBS in receiving touchdowns, Elijah Sarratt returns to the city where he went to high school with everything still to prove.

measurables.combineNote: Sarratt measured in at the Combine (6-2 1/2, 210, 10-inch hands, 6-3 3/4 wingspan) but did not test on the field in Indianapolis, so the athletic profile comes largely from Indiana's pro day, where he ran an unofficial 4.45 that answered the biggest question on his file and, per local reporting, pushed him up boards. The compiled testing line — 4.55 official, 33.5-inch vertical, 7.01 three-cone — reads average; the 10-inch hands and contested-catch tape are the selling points.

collegeCareer: Sarratt was a zero-star recruit out of St. Frances Academy in Baltimore who signed with St. Francis (PA) and immediately looked overqualified for the NEC: 42 catches for 700 yards and 13 touchdowns as a freshman, first-team all-conference, and straight into the transfer portal. James Madison got him next, and he answered the level-up question with 82 catches for 1,191 yards and nine touchdowns in 2023, earning first-team All-Sun Belt honors.

Indiana took him in the Curt Cignetti transfer wave and he became the identity of the program's rise. In 2024 he caught 53 passes for 957 yards (18.1 per catch) and eight touchdowns and made third-team All-Big Ten. In 2025, with Omar Cooper Jr. emerging as the alpha and Fernando Mendoza on his way to being the No. 1 overall pick, Sarratt was the team captain and the closer: 65 catches for 830 yards and 15 touchdowns, the most receiving scores in the FBS, plus a 49-yard game-winner with 88 seconds left in the win over Oregon. Indiana won the national championship in January.

The nickname tells you what he is. His father posted that Sarratt was 'always open, like a Waffle House' after another third-down conversion, and it stuck to the point that he sells merchandise for it. He is a contested-catch and back-shoulder specialist with 10-inch hands, a 72 percent career catch rate, 10.7 yards per target and 2.69 yards per route run in his final season — a high-traffic possession receiver who scored at least eight touchdowns in all four of his college seasons across three programs.

The limits are equally clear: he is 23, he ran 4.55 officially, he does not separate with speed, and his release package against physical NFL corners is unproven. He wins by knowing where the space is and out-competing people for the ball.

draftDayStory: Baltimore drafted Sarratt at No. 115 overall in the fourth round, one round after taking USC's Ja'Kobi Lane — back-to-back receivers, both big-bodied, both drafted to give Lamar Jackson catch-radius on the outside that Zay Flowers (a slot-heavy separator) and Rashod Bateman do not provide. Note the discrepancy with the KTC draft-capital line, which lists him as Round 4, Pick 15: the actual selection was the 115th pick overall. He was one of a program-record eight Indiana players drafted in 2026, a class headlined by Mendoza going first overall to the Raiders.

The story wrote itself in Baltimore. Sarratt played his high school ball at St. Frances Academy in the city, and he had not even been able to attend the Ravens' local pro day before the draft. 'It's crazy how things work out like that,' he said. 'I feel it's a meant-to-be moment.' The Ravens' stated interest was specific: they want to expand the back-shoulder element of Jackson's passing game and use big receivers like Sarratt and Lane as 'Joker' pieces in tight-end concepts under first-year coordinator Declan Doyle, who borrows heavily from Sean Payton.
whyTheyDraftedHim: Contested-catch and back-shoulder specialist with 10-inch hands — Baltimore explicitly wants to add that element to Lamar Jackson's passing game, which has lacked a true win-anyway target outside.

Size to play the 'Joker' role in Declan Doyle's Payton-derived scheme, running tight-end concepts from a receiver body alongside fellow rookie Ja'Kobi Lane after Isaiah Likely and Charlie Kolar left in free agency.
Four-year, three-program track record of production and leadership: a team captain on a national championship offense who scored at least eight touchdowns every season he played.
Fifteen receiving touchdowns in 2025 led the FBS, and the efficiency profile (10.7 yards per target, 72 percent catch rate, 2.69 yards per route run) backs up the scoring.
Hometown fit and character: a zero-star recruit from St. Frances Academy who has climbed every level he has been placed on, returning to the city that raised him.

campNotes.source: Jason La Canfora, Sports Illustrated (Ravens on SI)
campNotes.note: Sarratt was already the 'other' rookie receiver behind the social-media lore of Ja'Kobi Lane, but La Canfora framed that as a feature rather than a bug: no soft-tissue setbacks, daily practice reps, and a role built on dirty work that does not generate highlights. Sarratt: 'Just know every day's not going to be perfect.'

campNotes.source: Sports Illustrated (Ravens on SI) / Ravens PR
campNotes.note: Baltimore's first unofficial depth chart had Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman as starters with Lane and Devontez Walker as the second-stringers, leaving Sarratt outside the top four and fighting with Walker and LaJohntay Wester for the No. 4-5 spots.

Preseason debut against Philadelphia: six catches on seven targets for 66 yards, both team highs, in a 24-7 Ravens win, plus two punt returns for eight yards — and a third-quarter fumble in Eagles territory forced by Shaun Wade. He and fourth-round tight end Matt Hibner combined for 11 catches and 127 yards.

In the 13-3 win at Minnesota, Sarratt was among the Ravens' leading pass catchers with three receptions (behind LaJohntay Wester's five), including a catch-and-run first down from fellow rookie Joe Fagnano. Box scores differ on his yardage total for the night.

No reporting has surfaced suggesting Sarratt is a roster-bubble player — the questions are about his role, not his job. Baltimore's receiver room going into the final cuts is Flowers, Bateman, Lane, Walker, Wester and Sarratt for what is realistically five or six spots.

beatQuotes.quote: Just know every day's not going to be perfect. You're going to have ups and downs, but just continue to find those little ways to get better. You need to be coachable. Number one, you have to be coachable.
beatQuotes.attribution: Elijah Sarratt, via Jason La Canfora, Sports Illustrated, Aug 11

beatQuotes.quote: The back shoulder throws, that's a big strength of my game. You're always trying to win over the top, but it's a feel thing and then it's a trust between you and the quarterback. It doesn't happen overnight. It happens with reps throughout camp and practices.
I'm at ground zero right now. I have to prove everything.
It's a cool nickname but it's also a mindset, too. Like I said, those contested catches, I always feel like I'm open. It's just a mentality that I have.

1015.depthChart: Fifth or sixth in the receiver pecking order and playing for the No. 4 job. Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman are the starters, third-round pick Ja'Kobi Lane has been the toast of camp and is running with the first-team offense daily, and Devontez Walker was listed as the other second-stringer. Sarratt's preseason opener — six catches for 66 yards, both team highs — is the case that he, not Walker or LaJohntay Wester, should be the fourth receiver; his fumble and Lane's momentum are the case against.
whyHeCouldSucceed: Baltimore drafted him for a defined job: the back-shoulder, contested-catch target Lamar Jackson has never really had outside, in a scheme where Declan Doyle wants to use big receivers as Joker pieces after losing both backup tight ends.

He led the FBS with 15 receiving touchdowns and scored at least eight in all four college seasons across three levels — the red-zone skill that most quickly earns a rookie a role is the exact thing he does best.
His preseason opener led the entire team in targets, catches and yards, and he is also getting punt-return work, two ways to stay on the field while the depth chart sorts itself out.
Efficiency metrics back the tape: 72 percent career catch rate, 10.7 yards per target and 2.69 yards per route run in a national-title offense as a team captain.
The path clears fast if Rashod Bateman's contract or Zay Flowers' slot-heavy usage leaves the perimeter open in 2027 — Sarratt would be the biggest available body on the roster.
whyHeCouldFail: Baltimore throws less than almost any offense in football, and behind Flowers, Bateman and a first-team-reps rookie in Ja'Kobi Lane, the No. 4 receiver in this system can go weeks without a meaningful target.
He is 23.2 years old with an official 4.55 forty and no explosive testing marks; receivers who do not separate and are not young rarely grow into more than what they are.
Ja'Kobi Lane was drafted a round earlier, has been the story of camp, and plays the same big-bodied outside archetype — Sarratt loses that competition unless Lane stalls.
The Ravens' record of drafting and developing receivers is genuinely poor, and August practice buzz in Baltimore has a long history of meaning nothing by October.
He fumbled in his first preseason game, which is the fastest way for a fringe rotational player to lose the trust that gets him on the field on third downs.
fantasyOutlook: For 2026, expect a rotational role with spike-week touchdown equity and little else: something like 25-40 targets, 15-25 catches, 200-350 yards and two or three scores, contingent on winning the No. 4 job and staying in the punt-return mix. ESPN's own framing is right — he is best as a dynasty stash. The offense is low-volume by design, the two starters are entrenched, and Ja'Kobi Lane is ahead of him in both draft capital and camp momentum. What Sarratt has is the skill set Baltimore actually said it wanted to add, which is worth more than fifth-receiver profiles usually are.

In superflex .5 PPR dynasty, he is a third-round rookie pick — roughly where FantasyPros (22) and KTC (30) bracket him, and the right price for a 23-year-old fourth-rounder in a run-first offense. Do not pay a second-round pick for the college touchdown total. Do take him ahead of the sixth-round running backs and camp-body quarterbacks in this range, because there is a real if narrow version of this where Bateman moves on, Lane plateaus, and Sarratt becomes Lamar Jackson's 6-2 red-zone answer for four years on a rookie contract.
The honest read: high floor as a roster-worthy NFL contributor, low ceiling as a fantasy asset until the target tree above him changes.
1015.comp: A poor man's Michael Pittman Jr. — same contested-catch, big-hands, low-separation profile, same value dependent entirely on volume he does not yet have.
1015.bottomLine: A third-round rookie-draft stash with legitimate red-zone skill and a defined scheme role, blocked in 2026 by Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman and a hotter rookie; buy the price, not the highlight reel.
